content:
Apparently I’ve been busy.
I say apparently because when I look back over the last month, I can’t quite work out where all of it went. There have been phones to fix, English assignments to submit at least three days later than I was supposed to, exams to study for, a new monitor to acquire, a computer to rebuild, and somewhere in the middle of all of that I decided that what my life really needed was a fifty cubic centimetre engineering problem with two wheels.
The moped seemed like a good idea at the time.
This is becoming a recurring theme.
The last few weeks have been one of those periods where nothing individually feels particularly significant, but somehow everything happens at once. I’ve been fixing phones for people, studying for exams while simultaneously trying to convince myself that I had absolutely not left my English assignments until three days after the deadline, and putting together another computer after selling the old one to fund the purchase of something that I apparently decided was a sensible replacement for a functioning desktop.
Then I bought the moped.
It was cheap.
That should probably have been the first warning.
There is perhaps another reason I thought it was a good idea, and that is that I have developed a slightly dangerous amount of confidence in my ability to fix things.
Over the last year or so, I’ve had enough successes to make failure feel increasingly hypothetical. The Samsung S23 Ultra that had no business being recoverable somehow worked after the bypass. The ThinkPad BIOS problem that looked like a complete write-off turned into a working machine. The water-damaged MacBook Pro that Apple had effectively condemned came back to life for a handful of dollars and some stubbornness.
At some point, if enough things work, you start to believe that perhaps you are simply rather good at this.
That is a useful belief right up until you buy a project that turns out to be a complete money pit.
I am beginning to suspect that I am owed one.
The moped may be collecting that debt.
Buying an old moped is one of those things that sounds remarkably simple when you describe it in one sentence.
You buy the moped. You put fuel in it. You ride the moped.
Unfortunately, reality has discovered a much more interesting sequence of events.
First, I had to find the parts.
The particular engine in this thing isn’t exactly unusual, but apparently the exact combination of parts required to make mine work has become rare enough that finding them involves significantly more international logistics than I had anticipated. One particularly important part eventually turned up in England, which seemed excessive for something that had to travel halfway around the world simply so I could make a fifty cubic centimetre scooter move under its own power.
It arrived. It fitted. The moped ran. This was, obviously, the end of the problem…
It was not the end of the problem.
I bought a battery, got the registration sorted, arranged insurance, and finally reached the point where it looked like I might actually be able to ride the thing. I had reached that particularly satisfying stage of a project where everything seemed to be falling into place, and for a brief moment I could actually imagine myself simply getting on it and going somewhere rather than spending another evening searching for obscure engine parts.
Then it stalled while I was riding it.
Oh.
The battery was discharged.
That seemed reasonably straightforward, except the battery shouldn’t have been discharged in the first place, which meant that the charging system wasn’t doing what a charging system is supposed to do.
So began the next investigation.
Stator or regulator?
Regulator or stator?
Perhaps both?
I spent an unreasonable amount of time testing wires, measuring voltages, staring at wiring diagrams, and trying to determine whether the electrical system was actually charging the battery or merely pretending to.
Eventually, the stator appeared to be the culprit.
Excellent. Except I couldn’t find one. Of course I couldn’t.
The dimensions were just different enough from the common parts to make every search produce something that looked almost right until I actually measured it. Eighteen coils. Roughly the right diameter. Roughly the right mounting holes. Roughly the right centre opening.
“Roughly” is not particularly useful when you’re trying to bolt something to a spinning engine.
Eventually, after considerably more searching than I would have liked, I found one.
I bought it.
Now I’m waiting for it to arrive.
It could fix everything. It could fix nothing. The regulator could also be dead.
At this point I’m essentially waiting for a piece of copper wire wrapped around an iron core to tell me whether I’ve wasted another week.
The funny thing is that none of this is particularly unusual for me.
I think I’ve just become accustomed to projects behaving like this, partly because I’ve spent enough time fixing things that I now expect there to be another problem hiding underneath the first one, and partly because every successful repair makes it slightly easier to convince myself that the next impossible thing will probably work too.
A phone arrives with a broken screen and turns out to have three other faults.
A computer needs one component replaced and somehow ends up completely disassembled across my desk.
A moped needs a part and suddenly I’m comparing stator dimensions between engines I’ve never even seen in person.
There is always another layer. Sometimes that’s the fun of it. Sometimes it is considerably less fun.
And sometimes I look at the pile of parts on my desk and wonder why I voluntarily do this to myself.
The answer, unfortunately, is usually that I wanted to know what would happen.
Somewhere in amongst all of this, I’ve also been doing the things I’m technically supposed to be doing.
School, for example. Theoretically, I am a student. Practically, I seem to be someone who occasionally remembers that assignments have deadlines and exams require studying.
I’ve handed in English work late enough that calling it “late” has started to feel optimistic, although I did eventually hand it in, which I think deserves at least partial credit for persistence. I’ve been studying too, although there is something deeply ironic about spending several hours learning chemistry while simultaneously thinking about whether a stator from a completely different engine might physically fit inside my moped.
Apparently my brain doesn’t believe in separate compartments.
It just opens all the tabs at once.
Then there’s the new monitor.
I needed one. I bought one.
That part was thankfully uncomplicated.
The computer was slightly less so.
After selling my old machine to help pay for the moped, I found myself in the rather predictable position of needing another computer. So I’ve been collecting cheap parts again, gradually assembling something from whatever I can find for sensible money.
It’s not particularly glamorous, but I like building computers from mismatched collections of parts almost as much as I like fixing them, because there’s something satisfying about taking a collection of things that individually aren’t particularly useful and turning them into a machine that actually does something.
It also means I have another project.
Which, apparently, is important.
And then there is Bella.
She bullies me.
Everyone knows it. I know it. She knows it. I suspect she’d object to the phrasing, which is unfortunate because that only makes it more accurate.
She has somehow become the person I can tell about whatever ridiculous thing I’ve managed to get myself into, and despite the bullying, the teasing, and the occasional reminder that I am apparently incapable of making a sensible decision, I wouldn’t have it any other way.
I do, unfortunately, quite like her.
There, I’ve said it. She’ll hate that. Two can play at the game of bullying…
I’ve realised something over the last month that I’ve probably lived through dozens of times without putting a name to it. I fill space.
Whenever there is a gap in my schedule, I seem to find something to put in it. Sometimes that’s useful. Sometimes it’s productive. Sometimes it’s a five-dollar MacBook. Sometimes it’s an English assignment that I should have started three days earlier. Sometimes it’s a moped that I bought because I thought it would be a fun little project and have subsequently discovered contains significantly more electrical engineering than I was hoping for. I don’t necessarily think that’s a bad thing.
I’ve always liked being busy, and most of the things I do are things I genuinely enjoy, but there is a difference between having something to do and having something worth doing. I don’t always recognise that difference immediately.
Perhaps that’s why the last few weeks have felt so full. There has always been another problem to solve, another part to find, another thing to study, another machine to build, another message to send, another reason to keep moving.
And when everything is moving, it is remarkably easy not to notice that you’re tired.
The moped still doesn’t work properly, incidentally.
The stator is somewhere between here and wherever AliExpress has decided constitutes “nearby”. The regulator may or may not be dead. The battery is charged again, for now, and I am resisting the temptation to declare victory prematurely because apparently I’ve learned at least one lesson from all of this.
The computer is getting there. The English assignments are, technically, submitted. The exams are happening whether I’m ready for them or not. The phones are being fixed. And there are still five thousand things I’d like to do. So perhaps this really has just been a normal month.
A month of buying things I probably shouldn’t, repairing things that probably shouldn’t work, learning things I didn’t know I needed to learn, and spending far too much time trying to make a fifty cubic centimetre engine produce electricity.
It was supposed to be simple.
They always are.

title: It Was Supposed to Be Simple

content:
I’ve been left unsupervised.
That’s probably the easiest explanation.
Some people go for long walks when they have a quiet week. Others finally watch the television they’ve been meaning to get around to for months. Apparently, I buy water-damaged MacBooks.
In my defence, it only cost five dollars.
I volunteer at a local recycling shop every Saturday, where all manner of interesting electronics eventually find their way through the door. This particular MacBook never even made it onto the shelf. It came with paperwork from Apple in Singapore explaining, in admirable detail, why it wasn’t worth repairing. The recommendation was straightforward enough: replace the logic board, replace several other assemblies while you’re at it, and move on.
Most people would’ve looked at that report and seen a dead laptop.
I looked at it and thought, “Nah.”
For five dollars, it seemed worth finding out who was right.
Water damage has a habit of looking far worse than it actually is. Corrosion spreads, components discolour, connectors go green, and before long the whole board starts resembling something recovered from the bottom of Wellington Harbour. The trick is that corrosion tells a story if you’re prepared to read it. A missing voltage rail leads you to a blown fuse. The fuse leads you to a shorted IC. The damaged IC explains the burnt capacitors sitting beside it. One clue becomes the next, and eventually the repair almost begins solving itself.
Almost.
The actual shopping list turned out to be surprisingly modest: a couple of eight-dollar ICs, a handful of capacitors, and a fuse that came courtesy of my old ThinkPad T470, which suffered its rather undignified death by gravity several months ago. It seems only fair that its final contribution to the world was helping another laptop live a little longer.
I still don’t own a microscope. Just a pair of magnifying glasses, a soldering iron, a hot air station, and enough stubbornness to make up the difference.
A few hours later, I pressed the power button.
The fans spun.
The screen stayed black.
For a second.
Then another.
I briefly considered all the ways I might have made the situation considerably worse.
Then the Apple logo appeared.
I don’t think I’ll ever get tired of that moment.
People often assume the enjoyable part of repairing something is the finished machine, or perhaps the satisfaction of solving the problem. Those are certainly part of it, but they’re not what keeps me coming back. It’s those few uncertain seconds between pressing the power button and finding out whether the last several hours were well spent, because for a brief moment the outcome could still go either way. Everything you’ve done either worked… or it didn’t.
I’ve realised something over the last week, although “realised” probably isn’t the right word. It’s something I’ve lived time and time again without ever really stopping to acknowledge it.
Whenever life feels just a little quieter than usual, I make things.
Or repair them.
Or write.
Or start another project that absolutely doesn’t need starting.
I don’t think it’s avoidance.
Not entirely.
It’s just how I’ve always processed the world. Keeping my hands busy has a curious way of giving my mind enough space to catch up, and every project, no matter how inconsequential it seems, gives me something concrete to focus on while my thoughts quietly organise themselves in the background. Looking back, I’ve done this for years without ever really noticing the pattern. Give me an afternoon with nothing in particular to do and I’ll somehow end up with another repair on the bench, another CAD model open, another blog post half-written, or another idea that’s somehow become far more complicated than it ever needed to be.
This week has been quieter than most.
I miss her.
More than I expected to, if I’m being honest.
Not in some dramatic, world-ending sort of way. She’s away for ten days, she’ll be back in another five, and within about half an hour of seeing her again we’ll almost certainly have forgotten she was ever gone in the first place. The conversation will probably begin somewhere entirely unrelated, wander through three or four different topics, and before long it’ll feel as though nobody ever left. Order, as far as I’m concerned, will quietly be restored to the universe.
Until then, though, I appear to be coping by rescuing scrap MacBooks, proving Apple wrong one eight-dollar chip at a time, and pretending that’s what this week was really about.
I’ve certainly chosen worse projects.

title: Five Dollars Well Spent

content:
It’s mildly disconcerting, honestly.
Not dramatically so. She’s only away for ten days, and by the time she’s back I’ll probably have repaired something that shouldn’t have been repairable, broken something that was working perfectly happily beforehand, written another blog post, and somehow convinced myself that learning yet another obscure piece of technology is an excellent use of my time. Rationally, ten days is nothing.
Apparently my brain disagrees.
At precisely 9:58 this evening, my phone didn’t ring.
Normally there’s a reasonable chance it would. Not because we’d arranged anything, but because, statistically speaking, I was probably free. Likewise, somewhere around half past nine I found myself half expecting a message along the lines of, “How free are you on a scale of one to America?”
Instead, there wasn’t one.
It’s funny how quickly your brain learns patterns without ever consciously deciding to. You don’t wake up one morning and think, right, a phone call at roughly ten o’clock has become part of my day. It just… happens. One conversation becomes two, then twenty, then enough that your evenings quietly reshape themselves around the possibility of hearing your phone vibrate.
Then, one day, it doesn’t.
Not because anything’s wrong, or because anyone’s upset. Simply because somebody’s somewhere else for a little while.
The silence itself isn’t loud.
It’s just… noticeable.
I spend an unreasonable amount of time thinking about systems. Computers, radios, firmware—they’re wonderfully predictable. Give them the same inputs and, assuming you’ve done your job properly, they’ll generally produce the same outputs. If they don’t, there’s usually a reason, and with enough persistence you’ll eventually find it.
People don’t work like that.
They quietly become part of your routine without asking permission. You don’t schedule it, you don’t really notice it happening, and then one day you realise you’ve found something interesting and instinctively reached for your phone before remembering that they’re currently several thousand kilometres away doing considerably more exciting things than reading about whatever obscure rabbit hole you’ve disappeared down this afternoon.
It’s an odd feeling.
Not sadness.
Not loneliness.
Just… absence.
I think that’s one of the stranger things about memory. We like to imagine that we remember the important moments: the milestones, the dramatic conversations, the life-changing events. I’m not convinced that’s true. I think we remember habits instead—the ordinary things that quietly repeated often enough to become invisible. The phone call that usually happens. The message you almost expect. The person you automatically look towards before remembering they’re somewhere else today.
Those are the things your brain reaches for first, not because they’re extraordinary, but because they’ve quietly become normal.
That’s why I write.
Not because I think these moments are particularly remarkable, but because I know I’d otherwise forget them. Nothing else is ever just about the main point I make, and apparently this post isn’t really about a missing phone call either. It’s about realising that somebody can become such a normal part of your day that their absence doesn’t feel dramatic.
It just feels… statistically improbable.
The good news is that this really is a remarkably temporary anomaly.
In ten days she’ll be back, there’ll almost certainly be a phone call at some vaguely predictable time that starts on one topic before somehow ending up somewhere completely different, and within about five minutes the universe will have quietly corrected itself. This brief disruption to the statistical model of my evenings will disappear just as naturally as it arrived, and I suspect neither of us will think much about it ever again.
Order, as they say, will once again be restored to the universe.
Until then, though, it turns out that 9:50pm onwards has become a surprisingly interesting time of day.
Statistically speaking.
With love, Daniel

title: Statistically Speaking...

content:
It’s been a fairly boring week, which is unfortunate because those are significantly harder to write about.
School happened. Accounting happened. Physics happened. English happened. Another week quietly disappeared into the pile of weeks that came before it.
The interesting things all happened outside of school.
Last weekend disappeared almost entirely into the ThinkPad X1 Nano I’m writing this on now. What started as a laptop with no signs of life ended with me soldering wires directly onto a BIOS flash chip, reconstructing firmware images, and spending far too much time staring at hexadecimal data. By Sunday night it was working again. If you are slightly more technically inclined, you can read that one here
Monday and Tuesday were spent documenting the repair and finally setting up the website I’ve been meaning to make for months (the one linked above). There’s something satisfying about finally having a place for these projects to live. Computers are temporary things. Hard drives fail. Laptops get dropped onto physics classroom floors. Documentation survives slightly better.
Wednesday brought a new handheld radio. Thursday was spent programming it.
And then there was the Samsung.
I’ve been working on an S23 Ultra for the last couple of days. One of those projects where every solution leads to a new problem and every promising avenue turns into a dead end. The sort of repair that slowly convinces you that everybody else is right and what you’re trying to do probably isn’t possible.
In this case I was trying to recover a phone locked behind Google’s Factory Reset Protection system. Most approaches you’ll find online either no longer work because Samsung patched everything past Android 14 or require access to tools that ordinary repair technicians simply don’t have (or in my case, can’t afford).
I’d spent hours chasing ideas that went nowhere when another one occurred to me.
The phone was mostly stock, but there were a few firmware components I could modify, and others that matched the Android 13 equivalents ‘closely enough’. Nothing particularly dramatic. Just enough flexibility to try something I hadn’t seen documented anywhere else.
I flashed it.
The phone rebooted.
And suddenly I had ADB access.
That was the moment I sat back slightly.
The phone was still locked.
I still didn’t have a solution.
But for the first time all day, the device was doing something genuinely new.
Up until then every path I’d followed had ended exactly where everyone said it would. Now I had something different sitting in front of me.
It felt like progress.
I was on the phone with her at the time, which is not particularly unusual. The unusual part was that she’d largely stopped paying attention to what I was doing and had instead started scrolling Instagram.
There is a certain type of phone call we have where one of us is doing something and the other is just sort of present. Not really discussing anything important. Just existing in the same conversation.
She was describing reels. I was staring at firmware. Neither activity had much to do with the other.
Then somewhere in the middle of a sentence about something I have completely forgotten, I had another idea.
One of those ideas that appears fully formed without any warning.
I typed a command. The phone rebooted.
A few seconds later I realised it had actually worked.
I think my exact response was “Holy shit.”
The phone got dropped onto the desk because I immediately forgot I was holding it.
Hours of dead ends, and the solution ended up being a single line typed into a terminal.
The lock was gone. Just like that.
And now, somewhat absurdly, it’s my phone.
What struck me afterwards wasn’t the success itself. It was the feeling.
I’ve felt it before.
Four years ago now, back in Year 8, I was fighting with a da Vinci 1.0A 3D printer. A truly terrible machine which I loved completely.
That project seemed determined to resist every attempt at progress. Every solution revealed a new problem. Every breakthrough was followed by another obstacle. Looking back, I learned more from that printer than almost anything else I’ve worked on.
And throughout all of it, she was there.
Not helping, exactly. Not in any technical sense. Just there.
The funny thing is that if you look at the actual facts, these situations have almost nothing in common.
Different projects, different schools, different versions of me. Four years apart.
Yet somehow I found myself sitting at my desk yesterday with exactly the same feeling.
Hours of frustration. An apparently impossible problem.
And her voice in the background talking about something completely unrelated.
The rational part of my brain would like to point out that correlation does not equal causation.
She’s not secretly responsible for repairing printers or bypassing Samsung firmware locks. That would be absurd.
But I do find it slightly suspicious that some of my favourite project memories seem to involve her doing absolutely nothing and everything simultaneously.
Maybe it’s a coincidence.
It almost certainly is.
But then again, some things matter regardless of whether they can be explained properly.
Four years ago I was sitting in Year 8 fighting with a printer.
Now I’m sitting here writing on a laptop I repaired last weekend and carrying a phone I rescued yesterday.
A lot has changed. One thing hasn’t (for the most part).
That’s not nothing.
With love,
Daniel

title: I've Seen This One Before

content:
I got back from Auckland yesterday.
Six hundred and fifty-eight kilometres away from Wellington, if we’re being precise, which turned out to be just far enough for my brain to start behaving differently. Or perhaps it was the eight and a half hours spent getting there.
By the time you’ve seen the ninety-eighth farm on the same road, eighty-five kilometres since the last turn and another hundred and five until the next, you’ve had time to think, to say the least. And think I did.
The conference itself was excellent. Most of it was held in a fairly standard conference centre, which is considerably less exciting than it sounds when described that way, but the people made up for it. More importantly, I met the only two other young people there.
What I actually found were two nerds who occasionally managed to make my own level of nerdiness seem quite moderate by comparison. Usually I’m the one disappearing down obscure technical rabbit holes while everyone else slowly regrets asking a question. It was refreshing to spend a few days around people who could not only keep up but occasionally leave me behind entirely.
Yesterday morning, before heading home, we visited an amateur radio club operating from a historic World War II radio station. That was probably my favourite part of the trip. There is something fascinating about standing inside a building that exists because, decades ago, people were trying to solve exactly the same problem we’re still trying to solve now.
Humans standing in one place, attempting to communicate with humans somewhere else.
Different technology. Same objective.
There were cellular antennas on the site too, and enough expensive coaxial cable hanging around to make me slightly nervous, but honestly the history interested me more. The equipment changes. The problem never really does.
The conference was busy enough to be interesting but not busy enough to be exhausting. There was always something to do, somewhere to be, someone to talk to, but nobody particularly needed anything from me. It turns out that’s quite a rare state of affairs.
Most of my life is spent thinking about whatever is directly in front of me: school, projects, computers that are either broken or about to be, radios, things I should probably finish, things I should probably start, whether I can afford the next project, and whether I can get out of the next party invitation without offending anybody. The usual collection of nonsense.
But after eight and a half hours of driving and three days with very little demanding my attention, I found myself thinking about what I wanted to think about instead. Which turned out to be a rather different thing entirely.
We had a nice phone call while I was away, again nothing more than a regular catch up.
The odd thing was everything in between.
I kept noticing things and mentally setting them aside: a joke, a story, something ridiculous somebody said, a strange observation, something that happened during the day. Not because any of those things were especially important, most of them weren’t, but because I already knew who I’d want to tell about them later.
And that’s when I noticed something I probably should have noticed more consciously a while ago.
A surprising amount of my life consists of mentally collecting things for her.
Not because she particularly cares about amateur radio, computers, printers, conferences, or any of the other things that occupy far too much of my attention. She doesn’t. At least I hope not. If I ever hear her voluntarily discussing antenna systems or trying to learn most of what I know, I’m almost certainly being left forever.
But she listens anyway. Not because the subject matters, but because I’m the one talking about it.
And the more I thought about that, the more I realised I do exactly the same thing in reverse.
The thing itself doesn’t always matter. The person attached to it does.
I spent most of the trip thinking. The funny thing is that the more I thought, the less I found myself thinking about the conference at all.
Every line of thought eventually wandered back to the same place. Not because I suddenly realised anything. I’ve known for a long time now.
If anything, the trip simply reinforced what was already there.
Every interesting thing I see that I want to share. Every joke that only really works if she’s there. Every moment where my brain has already decided who I’d like to tell before I’ve consciously made the decision.
I keep arriving at the same conclusion from entirely different directions.
If feelings can be quantified at all, which I strongly suspect they can’t, then mine resemble a logarithmic function. Always increasing, never quite flattening out, growing more slowly than before perhaps, but still growing nonetheless.
A terrible analogy. But then again, most attempts to explain love using mathematics tend to be.
The truth is that I almost never say it directly. Not because I don’t mean it, but because it feels like one of those facts that doesn’t need repeating to remain true, even though at the same time it does. And honestly, I’m just not used to it.
Every now and then something gives me enough distance to think properly. A long drive, a few days away from home.
And every single time, without exception, I end up in the same place.
Not because anything has changed. Just because it was already true.
I know who my person is. I know who I want to tell things to.
And I know, with a level of certainty that is honestly quite alarming, that she is the only person I will ever love this way for the rest of my life.
If anything, the distance simply gave me enough time to put it back into the front of my mind.
With love, Daniel

title: Seven Hundred Kilometres (or there abouts)

content:
This was supposed to be a tech blog. Somewhere along the line it became something else, and I think we both know whose fault that is. I write these because she makes me, and she somehow enjoys reading my reflections on her, written about her, largely for her, in what I can only describe as an awkward third person that we’ve both just agreed to pretend is normal. So here we are again.
I’ve been thinking about thinking about her, which is its own strange loop to be stuck in. And I’ve been thinking about love, what it actually is, what people mistake it for, and why the word itself feels completely inadequate for what I’m trying to describe.
Relationships are social constructs. That’s not a cynical thing to say, it’s just true. The labels we put on people, boyfriend, girlfriend, partner, just friends, it’s all language we invented to approximate something that doesn’t fit neatly into boxes. What I have doesn’t fit neatly into a box. There isn’t a word for it that doesn’t either undersell it or misrepresent it entirely, so I’ve stopped looking for one.
What I notice, looking around at the relationships people my age throw themselves into, is that a lot of what gets called love is really just the performance of love. It’s showy. It’s loud. It burns bright and fast and then it’s gone, three months later, and they’re onto the next one having apparently loved each other completely throughout. I don’t say that to be unkind. Puppy love is real in its own way. But it’s romanticised to the point where it collapses under its own weight the moment the world pushes back even slightly.
Because love is not showing off. Love is showing up. It’s being present and actually listening, not as a performance but as a default. It’s the quiet, unglamorous business of caring about someone consistently, not just when it’s easy or exciting or new.
I think about fireworks a lot when I think about this. A firework is genuinely beautiful. It lights up the whole sky, everyone looks, everyone gasps. And then it’s gone. Ten seconds, maybe. Nothing left but smoke.
A candle is a different thing entirely. There’s nothing showy about a candle. But there’s the gentle flicker of the orange flame, and the smell of the burning wick, and the small amount of warmth it throws into a room, and it lasts for years if you look after it properly. The thing is, you have to learn to appreciate a candle differently. You have to be close enough to notice it. You have to actually look.
And here’s the thing people miss. Both have power, just released differently. A candle can light a firework. The firework is brilliant and loud and everyone sees it, but it needed the candle to exist at all. And as long as the candle is never extinguished, it can light countless fireworks over a lifetime. The people who are only the firework get one brilliant moment and then they’re smoke.
But find someone who is also a candle, and something else happens entirely. Two candles, steady and constant, lighting each other’s fireworks. Every brilliant moment between them exists because the flame was already there, patient and quiet, waiting. And because neither of them burns out, there’s no limit to how many of those moments there can be. Just two people, a lifetime of fireworks, and the candle still going at the end of it.
People tell me I’m boring. That I’m missing out, that I should be out there making a mess of things with a rotating cast of people I’ll have forgotten by summer. And maybe to them it looks like I’m standing still. But I’ve just figured out how I want to spend my time, and more importantly, who I want to spend it with. That’s not boring. That’s just knowing what you have.
She is not mine in any possessive sense. But she is my person. There’s a difference, and it matters.
My person is the one I can’t wait to tell things to. Not the big things necessarily, just things. Something funny, something strange, something that happened in the corridor that was so outrageous it was almost impressive. She’s the first place my brain goes when something happens worth sharing, which is most things, because apparently everything is worth sharing when it’s her. She’s the one I’m still thinking about when I’m trying to shut my brain down for the night, which if you know me at all you’ll know is not a quick process under the best of circumstances. She makes it slower and I don’t mind even slightly.
She is my stability. Not in a way that puts any of that on her, that’s not fair to anyone, but in the sense that she is a constant I have built around quietly and without really deciding to. The world is loud and things fall apart and people disappoint you, and none of it feels quite as heavy when she’s there. What we have is stable in the way that actually useful things are stable. Not rigid, not loveless, not boring. Just grounded. Rational in the way that a decision you’ve thought through properly is rational. Controlled not because the feeling is small, but because we’re both sensible enough to hold it carefully.
With love, Daniel
summary: This was supposed to be a tech blog. Somewhere along the line it became something else, and I think we both know whose fault that is. I write these because she makes me, and she somehow enjoys reading my reflections on her, written about her, largely for her, in what I can only describe as an awkward third person that we’ve both just agreed to pretend is normal. So here we are again.
title: On Love

content:
So much for posting every month. So much for “I’ll be updating this more.” Here we are anyway.
It has been barely over a week since the dawn of my 16th revolution of the sun, which feels like a reasonable excuse to finally sit down and write something. A lot has happened in a short amount of time, mostly involving computers going wrong and computers going right, which is on brand.
I’ll start with the bad news. The gaming laptop, the ROG, made a noise it shouldn’t have made. Plugged it in to charge, heard a whine, and that was that. Won’t turn on. Back it goes, almost inevitably, just to be at my loss in some way or another because that’s how these things tend to work out. At this rate I’m starting to think the only reliable laptop is a ten year old ThinkPad, and the only thing that kills those is a physics classroom floor. I would know.
The good news is I’ve replaced it with something considerably better for the money. I picked up a used desktop and I’m writing this on it now. i5-9600K, 32GB of DDR4 at 3200, an RTX 3070, and about 1.5TB of storage spread across an NVMe and two SATA SSDs. All of that for $650, which I maintain is the best $650 I have ever spent. It lives in a massive Cooler Master ATX case, which earned it the very apt nickname of “the big computer.” Relatively tasteful lighting, usually sitting on a solid blue or dark purple. It’s a good machine. I’m happy with it.
And then there was the birthday. Sixteen years old, one week ago, and the best gift I received was a water bottle. I say that without a single trace of irony. She got me it, and it stores carbonated drinks, I use it every single day, and I appreciate practical things more than almost anything else. At risk of sounding like an unpaid advertisement, it is genuinely one of the best things I own. She knows me well enough to know that a useful gift lands better than anything else, and she was right, which is also on brand for her. A useful gift from the right person is worth more than anything showy, which I suppose is consistent with everything else I’ve ever written on this site.
More soon. Probably. I mean it this time.
With love, Daniel

content:
This one is late. Very late. But it’s worth writing down before it gets any further away.
Last Sunday I went out with her. Coffee shop, then wandering around the shops, then back to the coffee shop because apparently once wasn’t enough and I had absolutely no complaints about that. It was a good day. A genuinely, simply good day, which feels worth saying out loud because those aren’t always as common as they should be.
The thing that stuck with me most wasn’t anything that was said or anything that happened in particular. It was just that for a few hours my brain was quiet. Anyone who knows me or has read anything on this site will know that’s not a small thing. The machinery that usually runs constantly, the problem solving, the overthinking, the running commentary on everything, just stopped. I wasn’t thinking about what needed doing or what I should have said or what comes next. I was just there, in a coffee shop, with her, and that was the whole of it.
There’s a specific moment I keep coming back to. Just sitting there, I was holding her phone and she was scrolling through reels, and I was just present for it. That’s all. Nothing remarkable about it on paper. But there’s something about being around someone you love unconditionally that just quiets everything down. No performance, no effort, just easy. I don’t have a better word for it than that and I’ve been trying to find one.
Being present is something I have to actively work at. I’m not naturally good at it. My brain likes to be somewhere else, usually several places at once, usually at least one of them being the future. But last Sunday it didn’t. She has a way of making the present feel like enough, which is not something I say about many things.
And yet the future only feels closer every day, and she’s in it. I don’t know the particulars, whether I end up in medicine or engineering or something else entirely, but I know that. She’s the constant everything else gets built around. The details will sort themselves out.
The way I care about her isn’t something I can easily compare to how most people I know care about their person. It’s not possessive, it’s not conditional, it doesn’t come with strings. It’s more that I would genuinely hate to see her fail, which I also know won’t happen because she is the most dedicated person I know. But she worries, and I wish she wouldn’t, and I care about that too. About all of it. About her being okay, and being happy, and getting everything she’s working toward. In essence, I just care. Deeply, simply, without much complication beyond that.
With love, Daniel

title: Last Sunday

content:
She asked for a post and I had nothing. Which is a first, sort of. Usually there’s something rattling around worth writing about, but today it was just this vague sense that everything is moving both too slowly and too quickly at the same time, and I couldn’t work out how to make that into something worth reading. Then I realised that was exactly the thing worth writing about.
I remember when school felt like a drag. My earliest writing, the stuff from two or three laptops ago now, was full of it. It started on an old HP Elitebook, moved to the ThinkPad, then briefly lived on a Dell Latitude I picked up because it was small enough to actually carry to school without thinking about it. I gave the Latitude to my sister when I was done with it, which was the right thing to do, but the backups of everything I’d written went with it. She’s still using it, which is good. The ThinkPad is still sitting around despite being broken, which is less rational but I can’t quite bring myself to throw it out. Too much history in a thing that size.
So the writing is gone. A whole HP Elitebook worth of it, a ThinkPad worth of it, whatever made it onto the Latitude before I handed it over. All of it. What I do know is that I’ve become a better writer since then, which I can say with some confidence because I was quite bad at the start and I’m at least less bad now. The loss stings less knowing that. A bit.
And now school just sort of happens. I sit in English and accounting and physics and spend most of it thinking about circuit designs or nothing at all, and then it’s over and another week has gone by without much friction. It’s not that anything changed dramatically. I think I just stopped fighting it.
The strange part is that the period I remember as dragging the most, the part that felt like it would never end, now feels like it was years ago. Which it was, nearly. I started writing properly about a year ago and that already feels like a different chapter entirely. Time does that thing where it moves slowly enough to be painful in the moment and then in hindsight it compressed itself into almost nothing.
University is two years away. Two years sounds like a long time. It isn’t, I know that already, I just can’t feel it yet. But I’m aware enough to know that when I get there I’ll look back at right now the same way I look back at the early writing I no longer have. It’ll feel like it went by quickly. It’ll feel like it was both yesterday and a very long time ago simultaneously.
I wish I still had those early posts. Not because they were good, they almost certainly weren’t, but because they’d be a record of what it actually felt like to be in the slow part. The feeling is still there in memory but memory compresses things, edits them, makes them softer than they were. Writing doesn’t do that. Right now I’m in what will probably look like the fast part in hindsight, and I’m trying to pay attention to it. That’s partly what this is for.
She’s been there through all of it, before the writing even started. There’s a story I tell sometimes about my first real 3D printer project, the one that taught me more than I bargained for, and the retelling of it shifts depending on who’s listening. Not because the story changes, it doesn’t, but because different details come to the surface depending on what the person in front of me cares about. Tell it to someone technical and it becomes entirely about the pain and misery of writing printer firmware from scratch, and she might not come up at all. Tell it another way and she’s quietly at the centre of it, though I keep that version vague because I don’t particularly want to field questions about it. I speak vaguely about her impact on my life not because it’s small but because it’s the opposite, and some things don’t survive being explained to people who weren’t there.
The point is she’s been a constant through a period that hasn’t felt constant at all. Everything else has moved and shifted and some of it has been lost entirely, three laptops worth of it, but that part hasn’t changed. That’s not nothing.
With love, Daniel

title: Slowly, Then All at Once

content:
Right. So. It’s been a while.
A few months of radio silence across basically everything. The blog, the socials, all of it. Life got in the way in the way it sometimes does and somewhere along the line I just stopped. Not intentionally, it just sort of happened. But I’m back, and I had a pretty packed weekend, so let’s get into it.
This weekend has been a funny mix of making money and spending it. About a year ago I started making 3D printed morse keys as a little side hustle. Nothing serious, just a way to scrape a bit of cash from the hobby. They were the first thing I ever sold, ever, and there’s something strange and good about making actual money from something you built with your hands. I kept at it for a while then drifted off, as I tend to do. Then out of nowhere this weekend three orders landed at once. Not life changing stuff, about $50 all up, but that’s not really the point. It got me back in the mood for it and that’s worth something on its own.
The timing also helped, because I’d just had to drop $300 I really didn’t want to spend on a new laptop after the ThinkPad met its end on a physics classroom floor. I was saving for a Vespa. A rubbish $1000 one, sure, but a Vespa nonetheless. The keys coming back at exactly this moment felt like the universe doing me a small favour, and I’ll take it.
While all that was going on I built a microphone for a QMX, knocked out a 3D printed colour coded cable organiser as a little design job, and took on a Kenwood TS-50 recap. The TS-50 came down from a guy in Christchurch who sent it to me specifically, which is always a nice bit of trust to have placed in you. These radios are old enough now that the capacitors are well past their best, so I pulled it apart and replaced the lot. It went back better than it arrived, which is true, but I’ll be honest, it’s still not quite right. There’s something in there I haven’t fully chased down yet. Better than it was, not as good as it should be. We’ll see if it comes back.
And then there’s the Ender 6, sitting in pieces at Zero Waste right now. Zero Waste is the shop I volunteer at where we take in donated tech and restore it instead of letting it go to landfill. The plan with the Ender 6 is to get it running properly and use it at repair cafes, printing whatever parts are needed to keep things out of the bin. It’s a CoreXY machine, theoretically faster and more capable than your average printer once it’s dialled in. I say theoretically because right now it very much is not dialled in, and I’m looking forward to every frustrating minute of getting it there.
Working on it reminded me of fixing the da Vinci 1.0A, getting on for four years ago now. That machine had no business being as much fun as it was. It was a terrible printer and I loved it completely. The Ender 6 has that same energy. But the da Vinci memory doesn’t just stop at the printer. It was also around that time that I met the first person who I just knew wasn’t going anywhere. People come and go, that’s just the nature of things, but every now and then someone comes along and something in your brain quietly goes oh. This one’s different. This one’s staying.
Which got me thinking about love as a concept. Not the greeting card version, the actual thing. I said to someone the other day that love and hate are equal magnitude vectors pointing in opposite directions. You can’t hate something that intensely without caring about it just as deeply. The intensity is the same, just the direction changes, which means in some strange way they’re the same feeling wearing different clothes.
I’m not great with words when it comes to this stuff. I feel things clearly enough, I just don’t always manage to say them out loud. An I hate you from me carries a lot more weight than it probably should, because it usually means the exact opposite, and I think the people who matter understand that. I think it. I imply it constantly. I just haven’t always been able to say it plainly. I’m working on that, slowly closing the gap between what I feel and what I actually articulate. This blog is part of that, if I’m honest. Writing things down and putting them somewhere outside my own head.
Oh, the joys of thinking like me. Can’t even look at a printer without ending up here. And yes, quite literally, when I say I hate you, I quite literally mean the opposite. I would very much like to just say it. But it would also be a bit unnerving if british boy suddenly gained the ability to process emotions. These posts wander all over the place, from capacitors to philosophy to whatever this is, but they all end up in the same place, written for the same person. This one’s no different.
With love, Daniel

content:
Nothing thrilling at all with this one, but if it’s visible after 5:40pm on 23/11/25 NZST then I have successfully implemented a much more automated workflow. This means I can write as much as I want, and literally push one button which runs a .bat script that pushes it to Github after prompting me only for a commit message. My server then has another script which hopefully runs every 20 minutes past the hour (3 times an hour, at :00, :20, and :40) if I wrote it correctly that should delete the old directory and automagically pull the updated copy from Github.
That’s all for now, this is just a test of my automation.
Update 6:22pm, the server-side cronjob isn’t running. Must have scripted it wrong somehow. I’m honestly more inclined to make a comically large physical update button at this point… The upside is now everything is technically automated, or at least I have to think less and I can just run two scripts to upload a new update.
Edit 12:12am 20/03/2026: I set this up but last time I needed to update something I ran the script on the server manually. So I have no idea if it works. I’ll leave my latest post just pushed to the repo and in a few hours I’ll see if it’s up. Should update every 10 minutes in theory. Also, now I just write in VS Code so I can use the git commit button because I’m a blog writer not a tech guy…

content:
3D Printing Resources A running list of the most useful stuff I’ve found while trying to get prints to not look like cursed spaghetti. Whether you’re calibrating, troubleshooting, or just figuring out what the hell retraction actually does, these are worth checking out.
🧠 Guides & Knowledge Bases Prusa Knowledge Base
Fantastic tutorials, calibration help, slicer explanations — even if you don’t use Prusa gear.
Teaching Tech Calibration Guides
Absolute goldmine for dialling in everything from e-steps to input shaping.
Cura Docs
If you’re using Cura, start here before guessing at random settings.
🛠 Forums & Help Prusa Forum
Super active and helpful — even the angry rants usually include solutions.
r/FixMyPrint
Post your disasters, get actual feedback. Sometimes even kind feedback.
r/3Dprinting
Big community, good for finding answers, inspiration, or just seeing what other people are breaking. (or being told “bambu lab just works” :P)
📺 YouTube Channels Teaching Tech
Practical, clear, and surprisingly in-depth.
CHEP / Filament Friday
Cura tips, Ender 3 fixes, and printable test files.
CNC Kitchen
Print strength testing, slicing experiments, and lots of “why” behind the “what.”
Got a resource I missed? Shoot it through — or better yet, let me break my printer trying it and write about it here later.

content:
This is the first entry in what will probably be a long running build log for the Ender 6 we’re getting up and running at Zero Waste. The goal is simple enough in theory: get a printer running reliably enough that it can live at the shop and be used at repair cafes to print whatever parts are needed to keep things out of landfill. In practice, as with most things, it’s been a bit more involved than that.
The printer came in supposedly not working, which is about as specific as the brief gets. Someone had already begun work on it before I got involved, following this Klipper guide for the Ender 6 as the basis for the build. So the plan was already set: Ender 6 with Klipper. I came in partway through and we’ve been working on it together since.
First issue out of the gate was the display macros, none of them were working. Had to dig into the config, modify what was there, and write new macros from scratch for the basics like purging and loading filament. Not the most glamorous work but it needed doing before anything else was going to make sense.
The printer did manage to produce a Benchy at some point, which counts as progress. Someone (me) got impatient and bumped the speed up to 800%, which is one way to find out where your tuning falls short. It needs work.
The bigger problem has been the BL Touch. The Ender 6 has a daughter board that handles connections for things like the probe, which sounds convenient until you realise it only passes through three of the five BL Touch pins. Signal lines, no power. The BL Touch needs 5v to function reliably and the daughter board only puts out 3.3v, so the probe was never going to work 100% properly regardless, though Creality supposedly thought it would have. On top of that, the original BL Touch had to come off entirely because the retraction mechanism had failed and it wasn’t retracting at all, which turned out to be a power issue for exactly that reason. Also, the probe on the printer originally had no cable with it, so we could not connect anything to the BL Touch at all.
I brought in my own BL Touch along with a cable, which solved the probe problem but left the motherboard end without a connector. I carefully removed the original wires hoping the plastic connector housing would survive intact, which it did, mostly. To reconnect everything properly I’ve ordered some pre-crimped JST cables to re-seat into the old connector body, along with a 5-pin JST cable as a backup in case the connector housing doesn’t cooperate.
The plan once the cables are sorted is to run some Cat5e ethernet cable or similar between the BL Touch’s connector at the extruder head and the motherboard, bypassing the daughter board entirely and giving the probe a clean 5v feed directly. That should be the end of the BL Touch saga, fingers crossed.
The cables have arrived. I’m back at Zero Waste on Saturday. More then.
(nearly two weeks later update- I had no time to work on this last week, and someone else may have the correct cable already going spare, so that’s that)
